title: Steven Levy and the Hacker Ethic (1984)
explainer: Long before "hacker" meant intruder, the word described the MIT students and researchers of the Tech Model Railroad Club and AI Lab in the late 1950s and 1960s, who treated systems as things to explore and improve. Journalist Steven Levy's 1984 book Hackers: Heroes of the Computer Revolution named and codified the ethic that grew out of that culture — access to computers should be unlimited, information should be free, mistrust authority — the same curiosity-driven mindset this module is trying to channel into something legal rather than something that gets you prosecuted. The tension the book documents, between that open-access ideal and the gatekeeping institutions eventually built around computing, is the same tension this lesson resolves with one rule: get authorization first.

title: The 414s and the Road to the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (1983-1986)
explainer: The CFAA didn't appear out of nowhere. In 1983, a group of teenage hackers in Milwaukee calling themselves "the 414s" (after their area code) broke into dozens of computer systems, including ones at Los Alamos National Laboratory and a Manhattan cancer treatment center, largely out of curiosity rather than malice. Their arrests and congressional testimony were widely cited at the time as evidence that federal law hadn't caught up with what was technically possible — part of what Congress was responding to when it passed the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act a few years later, in 1986. It's a concrete, real illustration of exactly the "I didn't mean any harm" territory this lesson warns you away from.
